content: In statistics, the standard score, also referred to as the z-score or normal score, is a dimensionless value calculated by subtracting the population mean from an individual raw score and then dividing the result by the population standard deviation. This process is known as standardizing or normalizing. The standard score quantifies how many standard deviations an observation is above or below the mean. It enables the comparison of observations from different normal distributions, a practice commonly employed in research. It is important to note that the standard score is distinct from the z-factor used in the analysis of high-throughput screening data, although the two are sometimes mistakenly conflated. The standard score, denoted as z, represents the distance between a raw score and the population mean, expressed in units of the standard deviation. A negative z-score indicates that the raw score is below the mean, while a positive z-score signifies that it is above the mean. Crucially, the calculation of the z-score requires knowledge of the population mean and the population standard deviation, not the sample mean or sample standard deviation. This means that the population parameters must be known, rather than relying on statistics derived from a sample of the population. However, obtaining the true standard deviation of a population is often impractical, except in scenarios such as standardized testing, where the entire population is measured. In cases where it is not feasible to measure every member of a population, the standard deviation may be estimated using a random sample. For instance, the population of individuals who smoke cigarettes is not typically measured in its entirety. When a population follows a normal distribution, the percentile rank of an observation can be determined using the standard score and statistical tables. In mathematical statistics, a random variable ( X ) is standardized using the theoretical (population) mean and standard deviation. Specifically, the mean ( mu ) is defined as ( E(X) ), the expected value of ( X ), and the standard deviation ( sigma ) corresponds to the standard deviation of the probability distribution of ( X ).
